questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes why Azure and AWS each independently converged on a five-pillar Well-Architected Framework, per Lesson 1?
options: Both vendors organize architectural quality around the same five pillars — Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence, Performance Efficiency — because both arrived independently at the same conclusion about what actually breaks cloud systems in production
AWS built its framework by directly copying Microsoft's published pillar names after Azure's framework was released
The two frameworks share pillar names only by coincidence and actually evaluate completely unrelated aspects of a system
Only Azure publishes an official Well-Architected Framework; AWS's version is an informal blog post with no vendor-backed assessment tool
The five pillars exist specifically to produce one combined numeric score, with no other practical use in a design review
questions.explain: Lesson 1 is explicit that Microsoft and AWS each publish their own Well-Architected Framework, organized around the same five pillars, not because one copied the other but because both arrived at the same conclusion about what actually breaks cloud systems in production. Both frameworks also ship a free, vendor-hosted self-assessment tool, which rules out the idea that only one vendor treats this as a real, supported practice.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D invents a one-sided picture the lesson never supports — AWS's Well-Architected Framework is just as officially published as Azure's, with its own free guided self-assessment tool (the AWS Well-Architected Tool), not an informal blog post. Treating one vendor's framework as official and the other's as unofficial is exactly the kind of mistake that undercuts the framework's whole purpose as shared vocabulary across both clouds.

questions.prompt: In the order-processing API scenario from Lesson 2 — a single-region AKS/EKS cluster backed by a single-region managed database, reviewed once traffic had grown enough to justify it — which option is written the way an actual pillar-anchored reliability finding should be?
options: "This design has no failure domain isolation above the pod level — a regional outage takes down ingestion, processing, and the database simultaneously, with no automated failover"
"This feels kind of risky to me and we should probably look into it at some point"
"The team building this clearly didn't think very hard about reliability"
"This system will definitely go down eventually, so the whole architecture needs to be scrapped"
questions.explain: Lesson 2 draws a direct contrast between vague language ("this feels kind of risky") and framework vocabulary that names the exact gap and implies the fix. Option A names the specific missing capability — failure domain isolation above the pod level — and the specific consequence — ingestion, processing, and the database all going down together — which is exactly what makes a finding actionable instead of a vague worry.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the reliability-vs-cost tradeoff Lesson 3 works through using the order-processing API.
options: Adding active-active failover roughly doubles compute spend, because two full production-capable clusters now run simultaneously instead of one
An untested failover runbook is meaningfully different from having no failover path at all
The right question in a design review is not which pillar is objectively "right" but what failure the business is actually willing to risk, and what it's willing to pay not to risk it
Cost optimization and reliability can both be fully maximized at once in the same design if the architecture is clever enough
A documented tradeoff explicitly states which pillar was deprioritized and why, instead of the deprioritization being assumed silently
questions.explain: Lesson 3 is explicit that active-active failover roughly doubles compute spend and that an untested failover runbook is NOT meaningfully different from having no failover path at all — testing is what makes it real. The lesson's repeatable question is what failure a specific business is willing to risk and what it will pay to avoid that risk, not which pillar wins in the abstract, and a mature review writes the accepted tradeoff down rather than presenting a fix as if it had no cost. No real architecture maximizes every pillar simultaneously — that's the chapter's central claim, not an exception.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a ________ is any line a diagram crosses where the level of trust changes — public internet into a VNet/VPC, an unauthenticated request becoming authenticated, or one account crossing into another.
questions.explain: A trust boundary is the specific thing Lesson 4 teaches an architect to hunt for on an unfamiliar diagram: every point where trust level changes, asking what actually enforces that boundary (an NSG, a private endpoint, an identity check) and whether that enforcement is visible on the diagram or just assumed.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly defines what a landing zone actually is, per Lesson 5?
options: A pre-provisioned, pre-governed environment that a new workload lands into, with identity, networking, policy, logging, and cost tracking already in place before the first application resource is created
A specific Azure product you install once and never touch again
A subscription that has been running production workloads for at least six months
A one-time security audit performed after a workload has already been built
A marketing term with no specific technical meaning in either Azure or AWS documentation
questions.explain: Lesson 5 defines a landing zone as a pre-provisioned, pre-governed environment — identity, network connectivity, policy guardrails, centralized logging, and cost visibility already in place before a workload's first resource exists. The entire point is that governance is cheapest to add before anything has been built, which is exactly what a landing zone front-loads.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the mistake Lesson 5 is specifically written to correct — a landing zone isn't a single product you install once; it's a pre-governed baseline built from several pieces (Azure Landing Zones' management groups and policy assignments, or AWS Control Tower's Organizations and guardrails) that has to exist before the first workload resource is created, not something installed and forgotten.

questions.prompt: Match each Azure landing zone term from Lesson 6 to what it actually is.
right: The automated, parameterized process of provisioning a new, already-compliant subscription
A container above subscriptions in Azure's hierarchy; policy and RBAC assigned here are inherited by every subscription beneath it
A subscription where application teams actually deploy resources
A subscription (Identity, Management, Connectivity) that application workloads depend on but never run inside
questions.explain: A management group sits above subscriptions and is where policy and RBAC assigned once inherit down automatically, including to subscriptions that don't exist yet. Platform subscriptions (Identity, Management, Connectivity) exist solely to be depended on, never to run a workload themselves. Landing zone subscriptions are where application teams actually deploy resources, inheriting what Platform already built. Subscription vending turns provisioning a new, compliant subscription into a repeatable automated process instead of a manual one-off, so subscription thirty is exactly as compliant as subscription one.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about AWS Control Tower, per Lesson 7.
options: Control Tower creates a Management account, a Log Archive account, and an Audit account the first time it's enabled
Service Control Policies are preventive guardrails that sit above IAM and can block an action regardless of what permissions a user has been granted
AWS Config rules block a non-compliant resource from being created in the first place, the same way an SCP does
Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) is the Terraform-driven equivalent of Control Tower's own account-provisioning process
An AWS account is a weaker isolation boundary than an Azure subscription, since most resources and IAM roles span multiple accounts by default
questions.explain: Control Tower's first guided setup creates exactly those three accounts — Management, Log Archive, and Audit — and SCPs are preventive, denying an action at the identity/API layer regardless of a user's own IAM permissions, even for the account's root user. Account Factory for Terraform is explicitly the Terraform-driven path to the same provisioning Account Factory's console workflow does. Config rules are detective, not preventive — they report after the fact rather than blocking creation — and Lesson 7 states an AWS account is a *harder* isolation boundary than an Azure subscription, the opposite of option E.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about choosing account or subscription boundaries by blast radius, per Lesson 8.
options: The boundary decision should be based on the worst case if an account or subscription is fully compromised, misconfigured, or hits a hard limit — not on who reports to whom
Security isolation, compliance scope, billing isolation, and operational access are the four dimensions that actually tend to drive a real boundary decision
One subscription per team always produces the correct blast-radius boundary, since a team's risk profile is the same for every workload it owns
A single shared account for the entire company ignores blast radius just as much as mirroring the org chart does, only in the opposite direction
A boundary drawn around "who needs access to this" is never a legitimate reason to separate a workload into its own account
questions.explain: Lesson 8 reframes the deciding question from "which team owns this" to "what's the worst case if this account or subscription is compromised, misconfigured, or hits a hard limit" — that worst case is the blast radius, and security, compliance, billing, and operational access are the four dimensions that actually drive where the line goes. One account per team inherits every org-chart problem (too coarse for mixed-risk workloads, too fine when a reorg happens), and one shared account for everything is the opposite mistake with the same root cause: ignoring blast radius. Operational access is explicitly named as a legitimate fourth dimension, not an illegitimate one.

questions.code:
az network route-table route create \
  --resource-group hub-rg \
  --route-table-name spoke-to-hub-routes \
  --name default-to-firewall \
  --address-prefix 0.0.0.0/0 \
  --next-hop-type VirtualAppliance \
  --next-hop-ip-address 10.0.0.4
questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes why VNet peering's non-transitivity is actually what makes Azure's hub-and-spoke pattern work, and what the route above is for, per Lesson 9?
options: Because a spoke can't reach another spoke through the hub automatically, the hub is forced to be the only path for cross-network traffic, and the route shown forces each spoke's egress through the hub's firewall so that single chokepoint can enforce one policy
VNet peering is fully transitive by default, which is why the route above is unnecessary in a correctly built hub-and-spoke design
Non-transitive peering means spokes must always connect directly to each other, and the route shown is how two spokes bypass the hub entirely
Transitivity only matters for AWS Transit Gateway; the route shown has no equivalent purpose on Azure
Non-transitivity is a limitation with no architectural benefit, which is why Azure recommends replacing it with a full mesh
questions.explain: Azure VNet peering is deliberately non-transitive — spoke A peered to the hub and spoke B peered to the hub still can't reach each other automatically. That's the feature: it forces the hub to be the only path. The user-defined route shown is what turns that non-transitivity into enforced centralized egress, pointing every spoke's default route at the hub's firewall so cross-network traffic actually gets inspected at one place instead of fifty.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B gets the core mechanism backwards — VNet peering is explicitly non-transitive, not transitive, which is exactly why a UDR like the one shown is required in the first place to force spoke traffic toward the hub. If peering were transitive by default, there would be nothing for a hub-and-spoke design to enforce at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an AWS ________ sits between a physical Direct Connect connection and multiple VPCs or regions, so one circuit can serve many attachments instead of needing a separate connection per VPC.
questions.explain: A Direct Connect Gateway is what lets a single physical circuit serve many VPC or cross-region attachments, per Lesson 10 — without it, an organization with multiple VPCs or regions would need a separate dedicated connection for each one.

questions.prompt: Match each DNS term from Lesson 11 to what it actually does.
left: Private DNS zone / Private Hosted Zone
Azure Private DNS Resolver inbound endpoint
Azure Private DNS Resolver outbound endpoint
right: Lets Azure VMs forward queries for specific domains out to on-premises DNS servers via forwarding rulesets
A private namespace for internal names, resolved only for networks explicitly linked or associated to it
Lets on-premises DNS servers query Azure private zones through a private IP in a VNet
The mechanism connecting a private zone to a VNet or VPC, which can cross subscription or account boundaries
questions.explain: A private DNS zone (or Private Hosted Zone) only resolves for networks explicitly linked or associated to it — a virtual network link or VPC association is exactly that connection, and it can cross subscription or account boundaries. Private DNS zones alone don't solve hybrid resolution; the Resolver's inbound endpoint lets on-premises DNS reach Azure private zones, while its outbound endpoint forwards specific-domain queries from Azure out to on-premises DNS servers — the same inbound/outbound split Route 53 Resolver uses under different names.

questions.prompt: Put these network-scaling principles from Lesson 12 in the order the lesson presents them.
items: Allocate non-overlapping IP address space centrally, before a spoke is ever provisioned
Provision every new spoke from a standardized, repeatable spoke template
Default every spoke's segmentation to deny spoke-to-spoke access unless specifically reviewed and allowed
Draw a clear ownership boundary between what the central network team owns and what each team owns inside its own spoke
questions.explain: Lesson 12 builds its four principles in this order for a reason: address space has to be planned before a spoke exists at all, which is only sustainable once a repeatable spoke template exists to apply that plan consistently, which only stays safe if spoke-to-spoke access is denied by default rather than assumed, all of which only scales past one team if there's a clear, explicit line for who owns the hub versus who owns the inside of each spoke.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes what a multi-Availability-Zone deployment protects against versus what a multi-region deployment protects against, per Lesson 13?
options: Multi-AZ protects against a single datacenter's power, cooling, or network failure, assuming the region itself stays up; multi-region is the only one of the two that protects against a region-wide event
Multi-AZ and multi-region protect against exactly the same scale of failure, just described with different vendor terminology
Multi-region protects against a single server or disk failing, while multi-AZ protects against an entire region going down
Deploying across three Availability Zones is, by itself, a complete disaster recovery strategy
A single datacenter's redundant power supplies make multi-AZ deployment unnecessary
questions.explain: Lesson 13 is precise about this: multi-AZ protects against losing an entire datacenter (a cooling failure, a local outage, a fire) but assumes the region itself stays up, since every AZ in a region can still share exposure to a true region-wide event. Only a multi-region architecture protects against that larger scale of failure.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D is the exact confusion Lesson 13 calls out by name — a workload spread across three Availability Zones is highly available, which is real and valuable, but that is explicitly not the same thing as disaster recovery. Multi-AZ says nothing about surviving a region-wide event, which is precisely the gap Lessons 14 and 15 exist to close.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ measures how much data a business can afford to lose, expressed as time since the last good copy, while RTO measures how long a system can be down before the business impact becomes unacceptable.
questions.explain: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) and RTO (Recovery Time Objective) are different questions, per Lesson 14 — RPO drives backup frequency and replication strategy, while RTO drives how much standing standby capacity a workload needs. A system can have a tight RTO and a loose RPO, or the reverse, depending on what the business actually can't tolerate losing.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about active-active versus active-passive multi-region patterns, per Lesson 15.
options: Active-active gets close to the best possible RTO because failover is essentially just rerouting traffic, which can happen in seconds
Active-active introduces a genuine distributed-systems problem — conflict resolution — when the same record could be written in either region at nearly the same time
Active-passive replication is bidirectional, so there's no real cost difference between it and active-active
A warm standby in an active-passive design runs at full production capacity at all times, identical to a hot standby
Active-active costs more by design, because both regions run full production capacity continuously whether or not a failure ever actually happens
questions.explain: Active-active's global traffic distribution means failover is just rerouting, which gets RTO close to seconds, but having the same record writable in either region creates a real conflict-resolution problem active-passive never faces. Active-passive replication is one-directional, primary to secondary, which is exactly what makes it simpler and cheaper than active-active's full duplicate capacity — the opposite of option C's claim. A warm standby runs at reduced capacity, scaled up only on failover; that's what distinguishes it from a hot standby, which already runs at full capacity.

questions.prompt: Put these resilience and DR decisions in the order Chapter 4 builds them, Lesson 13 through Lesson 16.
items: Deploy across multiple Availability Zones to achieve high availability within a region
Set RTO and RPO targets for the workload, driven by actual business impact rather than preference
Choose an active-active or active-passive multi-region pattern based on those RTO/RPO targets
Run a real failover drill to prove the design actually meets the targets it was built for
questions.explain: Chapter 4 builds in exactly this order: Lesson 13 establishes that multi-AZ gives high availability but not disaster recovery; Lesson 14 argues that RTO and RPO, set per workload, should drive every DR decision that follows; Lesson 15 uses those targets to choose between active-active and active-passive instead of picking a pattern on instinct; and Lesson 16 is explicit that none of it is proven until a real drill — not a tabletop walkthrough — actually exercises the design.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes an AWS Service Control Policy (SCP) from an AWS Config rule, per Lesson 17?
options: An SCP is a preventive control enforced at the identity/API layer across an entire OU that can make an action structurally impossible; a Config rule is a detective control that evaluates existing resources after the fact and reports compliance
Both are detective controls that only report on resources after they already exist
An SCP can be overridden by an account's own root user, while a Config rule cannot be overridden by anyone
A Config rule blocks a non-compliant API call before it executes, the same way an SCP does
SCPs and Config rules are two names for the exact same AWS feature
questions.explain: Lesson 17 draws the line precisely: an SCP sits above IAM and makes a non-compliant action structurally impossible for every identity in every account under its OU, even the root user. A Config rule continuously evaluates resources that already exist and reports compliance — the AWS equivalent of Azure Policy's Audit effect, detective rather than preventive by default.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D states the opposite of what Lesson 17 says a Config rule does — the lesson is explicit that "the default behavior is detection, not prevention" for Config rules, and that preventing a non-compliant action at the API layer is specifically the SCP's job. Confusing the two is exactly the mistake the lesson calls out.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an AWS SCP pairs with a tag policy by denying a resource-creation API call unless a required tag is present, using the ________ condition key.
questions.explain: aws:RequestTag is the condition key Lesson 18 names for the preventive half of AWS tag enforcement — the SCP denies creation when the required tag is missing, while the tag policy handles the ongoing compliance report that catches whatever the SCP's condition didn't cover, mirroring the Azure Policy Deny-plus-reporting pattern.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lesson 19 to what it actually is.
right: Pushing as much governance as possible into automated controls and reserving manual approval for genuinely novel or irreversible risk
Teams provisioning resources outside the sanctioned pipeline because the sanctioned path is too slow
A preventive, automated control enforced at the moment of action with no human approval step
A manual approval checkpoint where a human must explicitly review and approve a change before it proceeds
questions.explain: A guardrail is enforced automatically the moment an action happens, with no human in the loop — exactly what an Azure Policy Deny or an SCP does. A gate is a manual approval checkpoint reserved for risk that's genuinely novel or resistant to being reduced to a checklist. Shadow IT is the predictable response when the sanctioned path is slower than the problem it solves, and guardrail-first design is the chapter's actual recommendation: push as much governance as possible into automated guardrails and reserve gates for the small set of decisions that genuinely need a human.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about a functioning Cloud Center of Excellence (CCoE), per Lesson 20.
options: A functioning CCoE owns and maintains a shared, versioned Terraform module catalog so teams consume compliance by default instead of designing from scratch
A CCoE whose entire function is reviewing and approving other teams' proposals is functioning exactly as the name is meant to imply
Documentation, office hours, and onboarding material are real CCoE output, not a side activity separate from the modules it builds
The honest test for whether a CCoE is working is whether a product team consumed something the CCoE built, or waited for the CCoE to approve something they built themselves
The fix for a CCoE that has become a review committee is to add more people to that committee
questions.explain: A real CCoE owns the shared module catalog, the policy baseline, and the landing zone itself, and training/enablement are explicitly named as real output, not a side activity — a module catalog only pays off if teams know it exists and how to use it. The honest test Lesson 20 proposes is exactly whether a team consumed something built for them or waited on an approval. A CCoE that only reviews proposals is the anti-pattern the lesson warns against, and the fix is shifting the team's time toward building reusable modules, not adding headcount to the review committee.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) actually buys you, per Lesson 21?
options: It makes a decision legible to everyone who wasn't in the room, including a future version of the same team, by preserving the reasoning, the rejected alternatives, and the accepted tradeoffs in a durable, version-controlled record
It guarantees the decision it records is the objectively correct one
It replaces the need for an architecture diagram entirely
It is a tool exclusively for compliance audits, with no everyday engineering use
Its main purpose is to describe the current state of a system, kept continuously up to date like a wiki page
questions.explain: Lesson 21 is explicit about what an ADR actually gives you: a permanent answer to "why is it built this way" that doesn't depend on memory, a record of rejected alternatives so re-litigation starts from what was already ruled out, and an honest list of accepted tradeoffs — all captured at the moment the decision was made, by anyone who wasn't in the room.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E describes exactly what Michael Nygard's original ADR pattern was written to replace, not what an ADR is. Lesson 21 explicitly contrasts ADRs with "architecture documents that describe the current state of a system," which go stale immediately — an ADR instead records one decision, at one point in time, and is meant to be superseded rather than kept continuously current like a wiki page.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an ADR's ________ section lists the real alternatives that were on the table, including the one that was rejected — leaving it out and listing only the winning option is the single most common way ADRs fail.
questions.explain: Options Considered is the section Lesson 22 singles out as most often skipped or faked — without the rejected alternatives written down, a reader six months later has no way to tell whether a changed circumstance should reopen the question.

questions.prompt: Match each C4 model level from Lesson 23 to what it actually shows.
right: Class or function-level detail, treated as something a UML tool or IDE generates on demand, not hand-drawn
The whole system as a single box, showing the people and other systems around it
One container broken into its internal modules; rarely useful in a cross-team architecture review
The system's major deployable pieces and how they communicate; where most enterprise architecture documentation actually lives
questions.explain: Context shows the whole system as one box among the people and systems around it. Container breaks the system into its major deployable pieces — the level most enterprise architecture documentation should actually live at, per Lesson 23. Component zooms into one container's internal modules, useful mostly inside a single team's own design doc. Code is class or function-level detail that C4 itself treats as something a tool generates on demand, not something hand-drawn and maintained.

questions.prompt: An ADR describing a network topology decision is no longer followed, but no specific later ADR has replaced it yet. Per Lesson 24, what should happen to it?
options: Mark its status as "Deprecated" and leave the file in the repository, rather than deleting it
Delete the file immediately, since an out-of-date decision has no further value
Leave its status as "Accepted" since changing it would confuse the git history
Mark it "Superseded by ADR-00XX" even though no replacement ADR actually exists yet
questions.explain: Lesson 24's status lifecycle reserves "Deprecated" for exactly this case — no longer followed, with no clear replacement recorded yet — while "Superseded" is reserved for when a specific later ADR genuinely exists and can be cross-linked. The lesson is explicit that an out-of-date ADR should never be deleted; doing so recreates the oral-history problem Chapter 6 opened with, leaving a future engineer with nothing to actually read.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes why "Options considered" comes before "Recommended design" in an architecture review deck, per Lesson 25?
options: Showing real alternatives and why they didn't win builds credibility and answers "did you consider X" before it's asked, so the recommendation lands as a conclusion instead of an unsupported assertion
The order doesn't actually matter; review boards never notice deck structure
Options should always be presented after the recommended design so the audience isn't confused by alternatives
"Options considered" is only relevant for decks presented to a finance stakeholder, never to architects or security reviewers
Leading with tradeoffs and risks before any options are shown is the structure Lesson 25 recommends
questions.explain: Lesson 25 calls "Options considered" the highest-leverage section a review deck can include, precisely because it answers the reviewer's first instinct — "did you consider X" — before it's asked, so the recommendation that follows lands as a conclusion the room already agrees with the reasoning behind, not an assertion they have to reconstruct themselves.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E misplaces where tradeoffs and risks actually belong — Lesson 25's five-section order puts Tradeoffs & Risks fourth, after Problem & Requirements, Options Considered, and Recommended Design, not first. Leading with tradeoffs before the room even agrees on the problem or has seen the alternatives is exactly the kind of reordering the lesson says produces a meeting that goes sideways.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the question categories a review board predictably asks, per Lesson 26.
options: "What happens when X fails" is the single most predictable question a review board asks, tied directly to Chapter 4's resilience material
"What's the simplest version of this" is usually a sincere operational question, not an attack on the design's sophistication
Cost-at-scale questions matter because a design's cost curve can have a cliff from a tier boundary, an egress charge, or a licensing seat count, not just a steady linear increase
Appendix slides for likely deep-dive questions should be left out of the review package entirely so the board never sees them
A pre-mortem means walking through "what happens when this fails" with your own team, out loud, before the real review happens
questions.explain: Lesson 26 names "what happens when X fails" as the most predictable review question, and is explicit that "what's the simplest version of this" deserves a real, sincere answer rather than a defensive one. Cost-at-scale questions exist because a cost curve can bend badly at a cliff, not just grow linearly, and a pre-mortem is defined as rehearsing failure-mode questions with your own team before the real review. Appendix slides are recommended specifically so the deep-dive answer is one click away when asked — kept out of the main deck for tightness, not removed from the package entirely.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 27's three-part pattern for defending a deliberate tradeoff is restate the constraint, name the alternative and its cost, then invite the ________.
questions.explain: Inviting the counter-proposal closes Lesson 27's three-part pattern by explicitly asking the board to name what's actually changed, rather than forcing you to re-justify a sound decision against a vague feeling of discomfort — it shows you're not married to the decision while putting the burden of a new argument back where it belongs.

questions.prompt: Harlow Creek Logistics has three product teams and one platform team, but Lesson 29 designs eight subscriptions rather than four. Why?
options: Each product team gets separate production and non-production subscriptions for blast-radius isolation, plus three platform subscriptions split by function (connectivity, identity, management)
Azure requires a minimum of eight subscriptions per tenant regardless of team count
Eight subscriptions exist purely to match the size of HCL's leadership team
Non-production and production workloads should always share one subscription to simplify billing
questions.explain: Applying Lesson 8's blast-radius principle rather than the org chart, each of HCL's three product teams gets its own production and non-production subscription — so a mistake in a team's test environment can never reach that same team's production resources — and Platform splits into three function-specific subscriptions (connectivity, identity, management), for a total of 3 x 2 + 3 = 8, not the 4 a naive one-per-team-plus-platform count would produce.

questions.prompt: Put Harlow Creek Logistics' quarterly DR game day checks in the order Lesson 30 specifies.
items: Fail over Customer Portal to Central US and confirm the 1-hour RTO is met
Fail over the hub's shared services and confirm spokes in Central US can still reach the internet and resolve internal DNS
Fail back to East US 2 and confirm no configuration drift was introduced during the test
questions.explain: Lesson 30 runs the application-tier failover first to confirm Customer Portal's own 1-hour RTO, then deliberately tests the step most DR plans skip — failing over the shared hub itself and proving spokes in the secondary region can actually reach the internet and resolve DNS, not just that the firewall resource exists — before failing back and confirming the test didn't introduce drift of its own.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly explains why Prairiewind Underwriters' architecture review board approved a design that still failed during a real regional outage, per Lesson 31?
options: The review checklist was shaped entirely around application-tier RTO/RPO, so the shared hub network — which had no documented DR plan and was never deployed to the secondary region — was never put on the agenda as its own tier
The review board never checked cost projections or tagging compliance at all
The claims-processing database failed to fail over within its documented RTO
The board approved the design without reviewing network segmentation between spokes
Prairiewind's outage was caused by a security breach that bypassed every guardrail in place
questions.explain: Lesson 31 is specific about the root cause: the review board's checklist had a line item for application-tier RTO/RPO and no line item for shared network services, so the hub's firewall, gateway, and DNS Private Resolver — which existed only in the primary region — were never framed as a DR-in-scope tier at all, by either the application teams or the platform team that owned the hub.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C contradicts the case study directly — Lesson 31 states that the claims-processing database failed over exactly as designed, within its 2-hour RTO, and so did policy quoting. The actual failure was that nothing could reach the failed-over database or serve traffic, because the shared hub network it depended on for DNS and egress was never deployed to the secondary region at all — an application RTO being met is precisely what makes this case study's failure mode non-obvious.
